title: IB Failing Conditions Explained Clearly
summary: IB failing conditions explained clearly: learn the diploma rules, how IB grades work, and why 24 points alone may not secure the full diploma.
body_markdown:
A student opens their results and sees 27 points. Relief arrives first. The diploma requires 24, so the calculation appears simple.


Then someone asks about the Higher Level total. Another person mentions CAS. Suddenly, the number at the top of the page no longer seems to tell the whole story.


Here are the **IB failing conditions explained** directly: according to the IB’s current[Diploma Programme passing criteria](https://www.ibo.org/about-the-ib/what-it-means-to-be-an-ib-student/recognizing-student-achievement/about-assessment/dp-passing-criteria/) , a candidate needs at least 24 total points, but must also satisfy several additional conditions. These cover individual subject grades, combined Higher Level and Standard Level points, Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay, and CAS. Reaching 24 points by itself does not guarantee the diploma.


### The IB diploma conditions at a glance


For the full IB Diploma to be awarded, the candidate must meet all of the following conditions:


- Earn at least 24 total points.
- Receive a grade in every subject, as well as Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay.
- Receive at least a grade 2 in every subject.
- Receive no more than two grade 2s across Higher Level and Standard Level subjects.
- Receive no more than three grades of 3 or below across Higher Level and Standard Level subjects.
- Earn at least 12 points across the three Higher Level subjects.
- Earn at least 9 points across the three Standard Level subjects.
- Avoid a grade E in either Theory of Knowledge or the Extended Essay.
- Complete the CAS requirements.
- Avoid a penalty for academic misconduct.


This is why the safest approach is to check each rule separately rather than treating the total score as the only pass condition.


A student examines a results sheet with a magnifying glass while a parent studies it through an enormous telescope.


*The final total matters, but the conditions behind it matter too.*


### Following one student through the calculation


Imagine a student named Maya reviewing a hypothetical May 2026 result. The date matters because this is an illustration, not a prediction of future rules or boundaries.


Her six subject grades are:


Level Subject grade


HL 5


HL 4


HL 3


SL 5


SL 4


SL 3


The subject total is 24. Her Higher Level grades contribute 12 points, while her Standard Level grades contribute 12. She has no grade 1, no grade 2, and only two grades of 3 or below.


If Maya has acceptable Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay results, meets CAS requirements, receives all required grades, and has no disqualifying academic misconduct penalty, this profile satisfies the numerical diploma conditions.


Now change one detail. Suppose the Higher Level grades are 5, 3, and 3. Even if stronger Standard Level results keep the overall total above 24, the Higher Level subtotal is only 11. The diploma condition is not met.


That is the central lesson. An IB result is not merely one large total. It is a set of smaller gates.


### When 24 points can still mean no diploma


Students often focus on the 24-point threshold because it is memorable. But the threshold works more like the front door than the entire building.


A candidate with 26 points could miss the diploma because their three Higher Level subjects total only 11. Another candidate could reach 25 points but have too many grades of 3 or below. A third could have adequate subject points but fail to complete CAS.


Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay also matter. Together, they can contribute up to 3 core points, but an E in either component is a failing condition for the diploma. Core points can help a student reach the required total, yet they do not erase problems elsewhere in the profile.


Parents should therefore ask a more useful question than “Is the total at least 24?” The better question is: “Does every part of this result satisfy its own condition?”


### How IB grades and grade boundaries fit together


Each DP subject is graded from 1 to 7. A grade is not simply the student’s raw percentage written on a different scale. Assessment marks are combined according to the subject’s assessment model, and grade boundaries are then used to convert the final mark into an IB grade.


**IB grade boundaries** can differ by subject, level, component, and examination session. A percentage associated with a grade 5 in one subject should not be assumed to produce a grade 5 in another. Boundaries from an earlier session may be useful for practice estimates, but they are not a promise about a later session.


This distinction gives Maya a better way to think about her marks. During revision, she can estimate likely grades from an applicable boundary set. When official results arrive, however, it is the awarded grade and complete diploma profile that determine whether the conditions have been met.


For precise mark-to-grade estimates during preparation, use RevisionDojo’s **Grade boundaries tool** for exact conversions rather than relying on a generic percentage chart.


### A practical results-day check


When a results page feels overwhelming, check it in this order:


### Start with the six subjects


Confirm that every subject has a grade and that none is a 1. Then count the number of grade 2s and the total number of grades at 3 or below.


### Separate Higher Level and Standard Level


Add the three HL grades. The total must be at least 12. Next, add the three SL grades. The total must be at least 9.


### Review the core


Check the Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay outcomes. Neither can be an E. Then confirm that CAS has been completed, remembering that CAS does not receive a numerical grade.


### Check the overall total and status


Confirm that the total is at least 24, including any core points. Finally, read the official diploma status rather than trying to infer everything from the number alone.


If something appears inconsistent, contact the school’s DP coordinator. Schools can explain the result documentation and discuss the official post-results options that may be available.


### Preparing before results exist


The best time to understand failing conditions is before they become urgent. A student predicted 30 points can still have a fragile profile if one Higher Level subject is slipping toward a very low grade. Conversely, a student near 24 may have a balanced profile and a clear route forward.


Preparation should therefore respond to the weakest condition, not merely the loudest subject. RevisionDojo’s Questionbank and Predicted Papers can expose gaps under exam-style pressure. Study Notes and Flashcards help rebuild knowledge, while AI Chat can clarify ideas that still feel vague. Grading tools help students compare an answer with assessment expectations, and Mock Exams make it easier to practise a complete timed performance.


The Coursework Library and Tutors can support longer-term work when feedback and structure matter most. None of these resources changes the diploma rules. Their value is simpler: they help turn a frightening list of conditions into specific work a student can do next.


Maya began with one number and a vague fear. She finished with a checklist. That shift matters because uncertainty tends to make every weakness look equally dangerous. The rules show where the real risks are.
